metadata.title: When Is an AI Impact Assessment Actually Finished?
metadata.topic: AI IMPACT ASSESSMENT · WORKING WITH CLAUDE
metadata.purpose: Answer whether an AI Impact Assessment is done the moment Claude drafts it, or only once someone checks the draft against what the system actually does. Lands the carry-out that the assessment finishes with a fact-check, not with a draft.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carried unfilled '>' template placeholders at every skill-specific fact, and its named source_skill file does not exist on this machine -- see QUESTION.md. This redo reconstructs a generic, defensible AI-Impact-Assessment account from the title/family rather than lifting facts that were never written.

beats.narration_text: Someone asks if Claude can just finish their AI Impact Assessment. Wrong verb — Claude can start it; finishing it takes someone checking the draft against what the real system actually does. Liam, take it from here.

beats.narration_text: Here's the tempting move — read a fluent assessment and call it accurate. Now watch what fluency actually is. Describe a hiring tool as 'matches resumes to keywords,' when the real system also scores tone in video interviews. Claude drafts a clean risk section from that description — every category well-formed, every sentence correct to the letter of what you typed. The video-scoring risk isn't in it, because Claude only saw the description, never the system. They optimized language models for fidelity to the input text, at the expense of any check against the system the text describes. Fluent is a property of the writing. Accurate is a property of the fit.

shot.new_visual_element: A hiring-tool description feeding a risk section; the risk section fills in cleanly, then a caption reveals a whole risk category is missing because it was never in the description

production_viz.label: Fluent draft, missing risk
production_viz.mechanic: A short description card reading 'matches resumes to keywords' feeds into a risk-section card, which fills in with clean, well-formed risk language line by line -- fast, fluent, correct to the letter of the description. Once full, a caption fades in below: 'the system also scores video-interview tone.' The risk card's border flashes accent -- not because the writing is wrong, but because a whole risk category never made it in.

beats.narration_text: A working impact assessment is three fields, each answered against reality: what the system actually does, what data feeds it, who it affects. Claude writes all three fluently from whatever description you hand it — but it has no channel to the real system, no way to check its own draft against it. They optimized the drafting step for speed and structure, at the expense of any grounding in the machine the draft is supposed to describe. Watch the anchor: the hiring tool's assessment page, System and Data sections filled in from a two-line description, stamped 'draft — unverified,' because the description behind it left out the video scoring.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three labeled parts lighting in turn (system / data / affected people), then the hiring tool's assessment page stamped DRAFT -- UNVERIFIED

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- three parts, then the unverified page
production_viz.mechanic: Three chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a part of a working assessment (system / data / affected people), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. An assessment page appears with SYSTEM and DATA sections filled in ink text, a stamp across the corner reading 'DRAFT -- UNVERIFIED' in accent. THIS EXACT PAGE RETURNS, VERIFIED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Add the missing fact and the anchor page updates: the Data section is rewritten to include the video scoring, the 'unverified' stamp is crossed out, a 'verified' stamp lands in its place — because a human just checked the draft against the actual system. Now the two directions. A fluent, complete-reading assessment doesn't prove it's accurate; polish is a writing quality, not a fact-check. And a rough, half-filled first draft isn't a failure either — a scaffold that flags exactly what still needs checking is doing its job. Here's the trade-off: they optimized draft-then-verify for visibility over authority. The draft shows you what to look at. The verify step is what makes it true.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the assessment page's data section is rewritten and its stamp flips to VERIFIED; then it splits into 'polish is not proof' and 'incomplete is not failure'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- unverified, then verified
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 ASSESSMENT PAGE RETURNS, identical placement. Its DATA section text is struck and rewritten to add the video-scoring line, and the 'DRAFT -- UNVERIFIED' stamp is crossed out and replaced with a stamp reading 'VERIFIED' in teal. It splits into two cards: left reads 'fluent, complete-reading' with a struck-through 'ACCURATE' beneath it labelled 'polish is not proof'; right reads 'rough, half-filled' with a checkmark beneath it labelled 'incomplete is not failure'.

beats.narration_text: An AI Impact Assessment isn't finished when Claude writes it — it's finished when someone checks it against what the system actually does.

props.quote: An AI Impact Assessment isn't finished when Claude writes it — it's finished when someone checks it against what the system actually does.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm assessing an AI feature for impact and I want a first-pass draft. Describe an AI-powered feature you actually use or ship, in two or three sentences. From that description alone, draft the three sections of an AI Impact Assessment — what the system does, what data feeds it, who it affects. Then add one detail you left out on purpose — a data source, an edge case, a downstream use — and ask for a revision. Compare the two drafts side by side and list every risk category the first one missed. Go deeper: take the risk category that changed most between drafts and write the two questions you'd have to ask the system's engineers before you'd stamp that section verified.
